rv.q: Yet the unhinged underdog retains its essential charms.
It’s one of the many faces of resistance.
The opening of the cult hit “Titaníque”— the musical spoof of the 1997. Oscar-winning smash “Titanic” — is the latest theatrical evidence that one can be stupid and smart at the same time.
This is still a consistently very funny show, one electrified by a handful of true full-belt diva moments and unreasonably committed to its bit in a way befitting of Dion.

Mindelle clearly adores her subject in all of its Francophone campery and that sets the tone for a show that is impossible not to find amusing and that deftly manages to avoid reminding you even for a second that this was a disaster that killed hundreds of people.
“Titaníque” may be uneven, but at least it fits right in.
Titanique doesn’t just survive the jump to Broadway.
Now, amped up about as high as it can go with an all-star cast, Titaníque is guaranteed to deliver the most fun night you will have at the theatre this year.
Titaníque on Broadway is bigger than a mere hoot.
In moving to Broadway, Titanique proves anew that it's not only a silly good time, but also anchored by true comedic know-how and powerful musical performances.
Most importantly, Titanique is an absolute blast.

If “Titanique” gives off a distinctly amateur vibe, its goofiness is professionally honed.
But its appeal is narrow, and its comic returns diminish quickly.
Instead, I disappointedly report that Titanique—narrated by uncanny Dion lookalike Mindelle as an arch diva—is my idea of lowbrow entertainment at its just about lowest.
The entire cast is having a blast, and their infectious fun spreads generously to the audience.
Titanique has built the stage out, deeper into the audience and with steps, allowing the performers to come down to our level, racing up and down the aisles.
Titaníque, complete with that Frenchified accent to emphasize the final syllable, is one of the funniest musical comedies in years.
